required_work: Candidate leg for owner consideration: diagnose whether committed-transaction latency degrades super-linearly with chain depth, and whether that degradation is a product scaling defect or a test-harness artifact.
objective: Measure committed-transaction latency as a function of chain depth on the selected single-node profile, and determine whether the observed super-linear growth is a product-path defect (per-block work proportional to accumulated state) or an artifact of the debug-profile test harness. Produce the growth curve first; propose a fix only if the curve implicates the product path.
falsifiable_claim: Committed-transaction latency on the selected profile is bounded independently of accumulated chain depth; any observed growth is attributable to the debug build profile and disappears under the release profile.
selected_profile: The selected single-node deployment whose journeys commit real wallet-authority transactions against a local validator.

canon_snapshot.snapshot_role: Provenance for the canon revision this record was authored against. Drift detection is owned by generated/canon-baseline.v1.json via tools/canon-impact.mjs.

current_implementation_evidence: Measured 2026-07-28 on the selected profile, dual-system-projection capture (bootstrap-dominated, includes real wallet consumptions): debug 868s; release warm 329s, exit 0, 21/21. Release mode is therefore a real 2.6x improvement and the cost is substantially COMPUTE-bound, not wait-bound. The client commit-wait poll was separately measured healthy at 500ms (crates/cli/src/testing/rpc.rs).

Cold release run measured 1285s and failed one fixture self-test (malformed-readiness reap); the warm re-run passed 21/21 at exit 0, establishing that the cold failure was in-test release BUILD cost, not a defect in the IOI_WALLET_FIXTURE_RELEASE flag. Any future use of that flag should pre-build to keep build cost out of the self-test window.

UNMEASURED and the open question this record exists to answer: whether the same 2.6x holds on the DEEP consumption ladder. named-continuity restore measured ~5h10m against a 365s capture, and its cost profile (growth with chain depth) may differ from bootstrap. If release yields only a constant-factor 2.6x there, certification lands near 2h rather than the 30-60m target and the residual growth is still unexplained.
in_scope: Instrument per-consumption wall time against chain depth across a journey that commits many sequential wallet transactions (named-continuity's M1.5d dissolution ladder is the natural probe).
Compare the debug and release fixture profiles (IOI_WALLET_FIXTURE_RELEASE=1) over the identical journey to separate compute cost from structural cost.
Attribute the dominant cost to a named code path with evidence before proposing any change.
out_of_scope: Any optimization committed before the growth curve exists.
Weakening, sampling, or skipping any held-bar proof to reduce runtime.
Changing the certification-mode refusal of the checkpoint lane (that refusal is deliberate and needs its own owner ruling).
positive_proof: A retained latency-versus-depth curve for both build profiles, with the dominant cost attributed to a named code path.
adversarial_or_fault_proof: Predeclared: a flat release-profile curve falsifies the product-defect hypothesis and closes this record as a harness-profile finding; a curve that stays super-linear under release must name the per-block work whose cost scales with accumulated state, and is then re-filed as a defect record against its owning plane rather than fixed opportunistically here. The 2026-07-28 bootstrap measurement already establishes a 2.6x constant-factor compute component, so the surviving question is specifically the GROWTH term, not the constant.

code_anchors.evidence_scope: commit-wait poll loop (500ms, measured healthy); adjacent implementation precedent only; not proof of this work item
harness cluster/profile construction incl. the documented inert checkpoint_interval_blocks finding; adjacent implementation precedent only; not proof of this work item

remaining_nonclaims: This record claims no fix and no performance target; it produces a measurement and an attribution.
Certification wall-clock is a merge-time cost, not an iteration cost; the unit/fast proof lane already owns iteration speed.

The checkpoint lane is proven but bounded: it accelerates bootstrap-dominated journeys only (868s to 133s measured) and does not address post-checkpoint consumption cost (named-continuity restore measured at about 5h10m).
rollback_or_stop_rule: Stop and report if the release-profile curve is flat: the observation is then a harness-profile artifact and no product change is warranted.
exit_criteria: The growth curve exists for both build profiles, the dominant cost is attributed to a named code path, and the outcome is either closed as a harness finding or re-filed as a defect record against its owning plane.
source_provenance: Deferred from the proof-infrastructure leg (PRs #122-#124, master bd2dfc5f2) at owner direction, for consideration as a future leg. That leg delivered true chain resume and measured, and refuted, the premise that checkpointing could reduce certification wall-clock; it also eliminated checkpoint_interval_blocks (inert under GuardianMajority) and the client commit-wait poll (500ms) as candidate drivers. Updated 2026-07-28 with measured evidence: release mode delivers 2.6x on the bootstrap-dominated journey (868s to 329s, exit 0), so the remaining question is narrowed from 'compute or wait' to 'does the growth term survive under release'.
